case.case_title: Lakshman de Silva v. Hon. H. W. Senanayake and Another
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. (SLA) Application No.51 of 1989, decided on 4 December 1989

clause.text: Any accused person has the right to a fair trial and legal representation.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the accused petitioner was denied his constitutional right to a fair trial under Article 13(3) by being refused facilities (table and chair) to conduct his own defence and by being addressed humiliatingly during the trial.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner argued that refusal to provide a table and chair to take notes and keep documents, and being addressed as 'prisoner' by the High Court Judge, violated his fundamental rights under Article 13(3) to a fair trial and legal representation.
case_context.respondent_argument: The State argued that the trial had not commenced as per section 196 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and thus no violation of the undertaking to provide facilities had occurred. They also denied the allegations of humiliating treatment and contended that the petitioner was not entitled to the requested facilities before trial commencement.
key_facts: The indictment was received on 15.9.88; the accused was served and fingerprinted on 16.9.88 but not called to plead.
The trial date was fixed for 29.11.88; the petitioner was absent on that date but later conducted his own defence.
The petitioner requested a table and chair to conduct his defence but was refused by the High Court Judge.
A settlement was reached on 5.10.89 that the petitioner would be provided a table and chair during the trial.
The petitioner alleged breach of this undertaking on 30.10.89, claiming the trial had commenced and facilities were not provided.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court held that the commencement of trial under section 196 of the Code of Criminal Procedure occurs when the indictment is read and the accused is called to plead. Since this had not happened, the trial had not commenced. The undertaking to provide facilities was understood to apply only from the commencement of the trial, not during preliminary or calling dates.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found that on 30.10.89, the proceedings were not part of the trial hearing but a calling date, and the petitioner was not entitled to the facilities at that stage. The allegations of humiliating treatment were not supported by the record. The Court emphasized that the petitioner had not been denied a fair trial or legal representation under Article 13(3).
principles_established: The right to a fair trial under Article 13(3) includes reasonable facilities for an undefended accused to conduct his defence, but such facilities are required only after trial commencement.
Trial commencement is defined by section 196 of the Code of Criminal Procedure as the reading of the indictment and calling upon the accused to plead.
Pre-trial or calling dates do not constitute the trial for purposes of providing such facilities.
Allegations of humiliating treatment must be supported by the record to be upheld.
precedents_cited: Mohan v. Carson Cumberbatch & Co - [1988] 2 Sri L.R. 75

outcome.holding: The Court dismissed the petitioner's application, holding there was no violation of his right to a fair trial under Article 13(3) as the trial had not commenced and the undertaking to provide facilities was not breached.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 13(3) was central to the petitioner's claim that he was denied a fair trial by being refused facilities and treated humiliatingly. The Court's reasoning focused on whether the trial had commenced to trigger the right to such facilities, directly interpreting the clause's guarantee of a fair trial.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The Court held that the trial had not commenced as the accused was not called to plead, so the undertaking to provide a table and chair during the trial was not breached; allegations of humiliating treatment were not borne out by the record.
